---
title: User-supplied grammar (Java properties)
format: html
_quarto:
  tests:
    html:
      noErrors: true
      ensureFileRegexMatches:
        # Container marks the block with the language class, same as
        # built-ins. Tree-sitter captures from tree-sitter-properties' own
        # highlights.scm produce `hl-property`, `hl-operator`, `hl-string`
        # spans — these map 1:1 from the capture names in the grammar's
        # query file.
        - [!str "<pre class=\"sourceCode properties\"",
           !str "hl-property\">name</span>",
           !str "hl-operator\">=</span>",
           !str "hl-string\">example</span>"]
---

Quarto picks up tree-sitter grammars that are **not** built in but
live alongside your project. Drop them under
`_quarto/grammars/<name>/` with two files:

- `<name>.wasm` — the grammar compiled with `tree-sitter build --wasm`
  (or downloaded from a release asset).
- `highlights.scm` — the tree-sitter query file that assigns capture
  names to syntactic patterns. Its classes flow through to the HTML
  output as `hl-<capture-with-dots-as-hyphens>` spans.

Other files in the folder are allowed but not read: `injections.scm` and
`locals.scm` are not loaded for user grammars yet.

This document includes [tree-sitter-properties v0.3.0](https://github.com/tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-properties)
under `_quarto/grammars/properties/`, then uses it to highlight a plain
`properties` code block:

```properties
name = example
count = 42
```

Java properties isn't one of the built-in languages, but the user grammar
also takes priority on class collision — so you can override a built-in
the same way you'd add a new one.
